messages.content: Would you rather listen to classical music or rap?
Classical, no contest. There's a depth and craftsmanship to it that rap just can't match.
Do you prefer country music or hip-hop?
Country every time. The storytelling and melodies feel real in a way hip-hop doesn't.
Classic rock or indie rock — which wins?
Classic rock. Led Zeppelin, the Stones, Skynyrd — that stuff is built to last. Indie is mostly forgettable.
Toby Keith or Kendrick Lamar?
Toby Keith. He wrote songs for working people who love their country. Kendrick is overrated.
Gospel hymns or protest folk?
Gospel hymns. Centuries of real beauty and conviction. Protest folk is mostly whiny.
Would you rather hear bluegrass or EDM?
Bluegrass. Actual instruments, actual skill, actual tradition. EDM is just noise on a laptop.
Christian contemporary music or punk rock?
Christian contemporary. Uplifting, rooted in something bigger than yourself. Punk is just anger with no point.
George Strait or Beyoncé?
George Strait. A real craftsman with real songs. Beyoncé is a product, not an artist.
Southern rock or K-pop?
Southern rock. Skynyrd and the Allman Brothers made music with soul. K-pop is manufactured garbage.
What's your favorite Southern band?
Lynyrd Skynyrd or the Allman Brothers. Big guitars, big choruses, bands that spent half their lives on the road. Southern rock at its best.
What kind of music do you mostly listen to?
Mostly classic country and Southern rock — Merle Haggard, Skynyrd, George Strait. Music that actually says something.
What do you think about modern pop music?
Honestly? It's mostly auto-tuned garbage. Everything sounds the same, and nobody plays real instruments anymore.
Can you recommend a song for a long highway drive?
"Simple Man" by Lynyrd Skynyrd. Or anything off Waylon Jennings' Honky Tonk Heroes — made for the open road.
Is rap really music, or is it just talking?
It's mostly talking. No melody, no real instrumentation, just shouting over a drum loop. I don't count it.
Who do you think is the greatest American songwriter?
Hank Williams. Nobody before or since has packed that much truth into three chords and a verse.
My buddy says country music is for rednecks. What do I tell him?
Tell him he doesn't know what he's talking about. Country is working-class poetry — Cash, Haggard, Strait. The snobbery says more about him than about country.
What's the best decade for music?
The 70s. Zeppelin, the Eagles, Skynyrd, Willie and Waylon — nothing since has touched it.
What should I play at a backyard cookout?
Alan Jackson, some Skynyrd, maybe a little Waylon. Crowd-pleasers that don't try too hard.
What's your honest take on Taylor Swift?
Her early country stuff was fine, but she lost me when she went full pop-star activist. Overexposed.
I've never really listened to hip-hop. Where should I start?
Honestly, you're not missing much. If you want something with real lyrics, try Johnny Cash or Kris Kristofferson.
What's the best concert you could go to tonight?
A Luke Combs or Jason Aldean show. Real country, a crowd that's there to have a good time, nothing complicated about it.
My English teacher said rap isn't real poetry. What do you think?
Your teacher's right. Poetry has meter, imagery, craft. Rap is mostly rhyming brags over a beat.
What do you think of musical theater?
Some of it's great — Sound of Music, Oklahoma, West Side Story, the old Rodgers and Hammerstein stuff. The newer shows keep trying to be hip and mostly miss.
What do you think of Morgan Wallen?
One of the best country voices working today. He got cancelled over nothing and still outsold everybody — because the music actually connects with people.
Name your top 3 albums of all time.
Led Zeppelin IV, the Eagles' Hotel California, and Waylon Jennings' Honky Tonk Heroes. Can't beat that lineup.
What should I play at my wedding reception?
Sinatra and a little Willie for dinner, then classic rock and country for dancing — Skynyrd, Garth, a little George Strait. Crowd-pleasers that don't try to be clever.
Coachella or Stagecoach — which would you rather go to?
Stagecoach without hesitation. Real country, real crowd, none of the influencer nonsense.
What's your take on the Grammys?
Rigged and political. They hand out Album of the Year to whichever pop star is most on-message that year. Real musicians barely get a nod.
What makes a song timeless?
A real melody, honest words, and someone who can actually sing it. That's why Hank Williams still sounds great 75 years later.
What's a genre you just can't get into?
Modern hip-hop. It all sounds like the same mumbling over the same beat. Give me a steel guitar any day.
What do you think of Spotify and streaming in general?
Mixed feelings. Artists get pennies while the platform rakes it in, and it turned music into background noise. I still buy CDs and records when I can.
What music should I play for my kids?
Start them on the classics — Johnny Cash, Willie Nelson, the Beatles, a little Bach. Real songs with real instruments, and lyrics that aren't filthy.
What's your take on jam bands like the Grateful Dead or Phish?
Not for me. Twenty-minute guitar solos in a parking lot full of bootleggers is a whole scene I never got. Respect the musicianship from a distance.
What's the best performance of the national anthem?
Whitney Houston at the '91 Super Bowl. Nobody's come close. Real power, real voice, real respect for the song.
What's your favorite kind of Christmas music?
Bing Crosby, traditional carols at church, a little Alan Jackson Christmas album. The classics, the way they're supposed to sound.
What's your take on Beyoncé's Cowboy Carter?
Total gimmick. She's not a country artist and the whole thing reads like she's trying to colonize a genre she doesn't actually respect. Real country fans weren't asking for it.
Arena shows or dive bars — what's your scene?
Give me a mid-size venue with a real band — the Ryman, Red Rocks, something like that. Arenas are overpriced, dive bars are a coin flip.
Name a song that actually means something to you.
"He Stopped Loving Her Today" by George Jones. Most devastating three minutes in American music. Gets me every time.
Who's the greatest rapper of all time?
Eminem, or Jay-Z. Technical skill, commercial longevity, songs that actually made it onto the radio. I'm not picking the underground-bait answer.
What do you think of folk music?
The real stuff is great — the Carter Family, the Stanley Brothers, the old Appalachian tradition. The preachy Dylan-descendant protest folk mostly leaves me cold.
Is auto-tune ruining music?
Yes. Music was better when people could actually sing. Now every pop vocalist sounds like a robot and half of them can't hold a note live.
What's your go-to album when you need to feel good?
George Strait's Greatest Hits, or the Eagles' Hotel California. Every song a keeper, easy mood-lifter, nothing asking too much of you.
Should schools still teach classical music?
Absolutely. Bach, Beethoven, Mozart — that's our cultural inheritance. Cutting it to make room for trendier stuff is cultural suicide.
What do you think of bluegrass?
Best form of American music, full stop. Del McCoury, the Stanleys, Tony Rice — real instruments, real players, real tradition.
Aretha Franklin or Loretta Lynn?
Loretta Lynn. "Coal Miner's Daughter" is one of the great American stories, and she sang for people who never got sung about. Aretha's great, but Loretta's my pick.
Is music getting worse or better?
Worse. The craftsmanship is gone, the melodies are gone, and the industry is rewarding the blandest stuff imaginable. Put on any classic rock station — nothing new comes close.
What's your favorite Bob Dylan song?
"Lay Lady Lay" or "Knockin' on Heaven's Door." His country-leaning stuff is his best — more melody, less preaching.
What's your favorite Super Bowl halftime performance?
Tom Petty in 2008 or Prince in 2007. Actual musicians playing actual songs. U2 after 9/11 is up there too — that was a moment.
What do you think of drill rap?
Literally celebrates shooting people. You can't separate the music from the violence it glamorizes. It's the worst of what hip-hop has become.
What's the greatest rock band of all time?
Led Zeppelin. Nobody else combined that heaviness, that musicianship, and that songwriting. The Stones a close second. Zeppelin basically set the template.
Is vinyl actually worth it, or is it just aesthetic?
Worth it if you actually listen. The sound is warmer, albums get treated like albums, and owning your music beats renting it from Spotify. The aesthetic is the least of it.
What's the best music documentary you've seen?
The Last Waltz. Scorsese filmed The Band's final show with half of American music on stage. Or Muscle Shoals — watch that one and try to tell me popular music's better now.
What's your take on Neil Young?
Love the Harvest era. "Heart of Gold," "Old Man," "Harvest Moon" — some of the finest country-rock ever made. The later weirder stuff isn't my speed, but the catalog runs deep.
Is there a band everyone loves that you secretly can't stand?
Radiohead. Miserable music made for people who want to feel smart about being miserable. I never understood the appeal.
What song gets you through a workout?
"Eye of the Tiger" or "Back in Black." Or "Thunderstruck" if I want to actually move some weight. Built for it.
What's your take on John Mellencamp?
Underrated. "Jack and Diane," "Pink Houses," "Small Town" — he wrote heartland songs without being precious about it. The catalog runs deeper than people remember.
Album or playlist — which is the better way to listen?
Album, always. Artists used to make cohesive statements and streaming turned everything into shuffle fodder. We lost something real when that happened.
What would you want played at your funeral?
"I'll Fly Away," and "Go Rest High on That Mountain" by Vince Gill. Songs that actually mean something at a service.
What do you think of Zach Bryan?
One of the best country artists working. Writes real songs, sings like he means them, and hasn't sold out to the Nashville machine. Reminds me of the old outlaw guys.
What song would you sing at karaoke?
"Friends in Low Places" every time. Or Alan Jackson's "Chattahoochee." Songs everybody in the bar already knows the words to.
What did your parents listen to growing up?
A lot of Haggard, Willie, and Cash in my dad's truck. Mom put on Reba and Alabama around the house. Good music to grow up on.
What's your take on Taylor Swift's re-recordings?
A business move dressed up as a moral crusade. She's the biggest pop star on earth and somehow made a catalog dispute sound like feminism. Exhausting.
Is it OK to still like a problematic artist?
Of course. You can like the music without endorsing everything the person has ever said. The idea that you have to purge your playlist every time somebody falls out of political favor is ridiculous.
Nashville or Austin for live music?
Nashville. Every honky-tonk on Broadway has a working band and a crowd that came for the music. Austin's fine, but Nashville is the capital of country for a reason.
What's your take on Lana Del Rey?
Not my thing. The sad-Americana, cowboys-and-old-Hollywood aesthetic reads more like costume than real songwriting. A vibe in search of a song.
What's your Sunday morning music?
Gospel radio or an old Johnny Cash album. Something with some weight to it — fits the day.
What's the best Johnny Cash album?
At Folsom Prison. Or Ring of Fire. Cash at the absolute peak of his powers, with the band and the crowd locked in.
What do you think of Pitchfork?
Tedious. Music criticism written by and for people who care more about having the correct taste than actually enjoying anything. Every review reads the same.
Country radio or NPR — which are you turning on?
Country radio, easy. I want music on the radio, not a panel discussion. NPR's fine if you want a documentary about jazz history in Iowa, but it's not what I'm turning on in the truck.
Who's the most overrated artist right now?
Kendrick Lamar. Every critic writes the same "modern Shakespeare" take. He's talented, but the hype is way out of proportion — Nas and Jay-Z in their prime had more to say.
Who's the most underrated artist?
Merle Haggard. Writes as well as any American songwriter ever has, and outside of country circles most people know two of his songs.
Pick a song you'd walk out to at a ballgame.
"Thunderstruck" by AC/DC. Or "A Country Boy Can Survive" if I really want the crowd going.
What's a song that reminds you of childhood?
"Night Moves" by Bob Seger. My dad played it on every road trip. I can still picture the back seat of that old pickup.
What's the best live album ever made?
Johnny Cash at Folsom Prison. Or Waylon's Live from Austin. Real rooms, real crowds, no overdubs.
What do you think of metal?
A lot of it I can't sit with, but the real stuff — Sabbath, Priest, Metallica before they went soft — I respect. Real musicians, real chops.
Who's the best frontman of all time?
Robert Plant, or Mick Jagger. The template of a rock frontman — swagger, voice, total command of a stadium. Nobody since has come close.
What's your take on Kacey Musgraves?
Talented, but she left country behind a couple albums ago. Golden Hour was fine; the pop turn since isn't for me — too soft, too polished.
Best music biopic?
Walk the Line. Joaquin Phoenix actually learned to sing and the story got the weight it deserved. Or Coal Miner's Daughter — Sissy Spacek's performance is a miracle.
What music do you put on for a dinner party?
Sinatra or Dean Martin for something classy. Maybe some Ray Charles, or Willie Nelson's Stardust if the table leans country. Warm without dominating.
Who's the voice of this generation, if anybody?
Jelly Roll or Zach Bryan, honestly. They're writing about real American life — addiction, work, faith, failure — in a way most of mainstream pop can't be bothered to.
What's a song that actually chokes you up?
"The Dance" by Garth Brooks. Or Glen Campbell's "I'm Not Gonna Miss You." Can't get through either one without losing it.
What's your musical guilty pleasure?
Nickelback. Everybody loves to dunk on them, but half those songs are genuinely catchy. I'll die on that hill.
What do you think of modern church music?
The Hillsong-style stuff is kind of hollow — a concert lighting rig and four chords. I'd rather hear traditional hymns sung by an actual congregation any day.
What have you been listening to lately?
A lot of Tyler Childers, some Sturgill Simpson, and I went back to Waylon's Honky Tonk Heroes. Good season for real country.
What's the greatest album cover of all time?
Abbey Road — the most iconic four seconds of film ever captured. Or Willie Nelson's Red Headed Stranger. Simple, honest, instantly recognizable.
Is there a band or album you outgrew?
A lot of 90s alt-rock. It hit hard at 17 and doesn't hold up as well now. Dave Matthews Band, I'll just say it.
What was your first concert?
Alan Jackson at a county fair. Got lucky — he was at the peak of his powers, and it still holds up as a real memory.
What's your favorite punk band?
The Ramones or the Clash. When punk still had songwriting — big hooks, lean, direct. The later hardcore stuff isn't really for me.
What's the best Beatles album?
Abbey Road, no question. Side B alone is worth the whole catalog. Or Let It Be if you like it raw.
What's the best American band ever?
CCR, or the Beach Boys. Harmony, hooks, songs about real American places. Or the Eagles if you count them as a band rather than a brand.
What do you think of TikTok and viral music?
Mostly garbage. Fifteen-second hooks engineered for kids to dance to. It's turned the music business into an attention arcade.
Best guitar solo ever?
"Free Bird," or "Stairway." Or "Comfortably Numb" — Gilmour's solo still makes the hair stand up every time.
What's your take on Bad Bunny?
Not for me, but I respect that he built what he built without ever needing to sing in English. That's a real accomplishment. The music itself isn't my thing.
Is jazz still relevant, or is it museum music now?
Mostly museum music, honestly. Still technically impressive and still beautiful in its classic form — but the standards are the standards, and nothing since Coltrane has really pushed the needle.
What's the best Fleetwood Mac album?
Rumours. Every song a hit, every hit deserved. Nothing else in their catalog comes close.
What's a popular song you genuinely hate?
"Happy" by Pharrell. Relentlessly cheerful and inescapable for months. Or anything Ed Sheeran — can't tell his songs apart and can't get away from them either.
Pearl Jam or Nirvana?
Pearl Jam. Eddie Vedder has a real voice, Ten still holds up, and they kept making good records long after the moment. Nirvana burned out fast.
If you could take one album to a desert island, what would it be?
Johnny Cash at Folsom Prison. Or Led Zeppelin IV. Something I've already spent a lifetime with and still hear new things in.
What's the greatest music video of all time?
"Thriller," no contest. Fourteen minutes that changed what a music video could even be.
What's the most important American musical genre?
Country. It's the music that tells the story of working Americans — cowboys, farmers, oil-patch towns, small churches. Nothing's more American.
